topic: How to meet the FoodShare work requirement
section_heading: How do I meet the FoodShare work requirement?
passage:
There are three main ways to meet the work requirement.
Working or volunteering at least 80 hours per month.
Participating in a work training program at least 80 hours per month. Work programs include FoodShare Employment and Training (FSET) , Job Corps, Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) training programs through your local job center, Transitional Jobs, and Transform Milwaukee Jobs.
Working, volunteering, and taking part in a work program for a combined total of at least 80 hours each month.

topic: Definition of exemptions from the work requirement
section_heading: What are exemptions to the work requirement?
passage: Exemptions are reasons why you don’t have to meet the work requirement under federal law. At your interview, your local agency will check to see if you have an exemption. Reach out to your local agency right away if you think you have an exemption. Or, report an exemption in your ACCESS ( ACCESS in Spanish ) account.

topic: Who is exempt from the work requirement
passage:
You don't have meet the work requirement if:
You are pregnant.
You can't work due to your physical or mental health. This includes if you can’t work because you are experiencing homelessness.
You are living with a child who is 13 years old or younger, even if the child is not eligible for FoodShare.
You are Tribal member.
You care for a child aged 5 or younger who doesn’t live with you.
You care for a person who can’t care for themself (whether the person lives in or out of your home).
You are getting or applied for unemployment compensation.
You are in a school, training program, or college at least half-time.
You are participating in W-2.
You are in an alcohol or other drug abuse (AODA) treatment or rehabilitation program.

topic: What good cause means for the work requirement
section_heading: What if something happens and I can't make 80 hours in a month?
passage: If something happens in your life that you cannot control, like you get sick or your car breaks down and you can't meet the work requirement's 80 hours in a month, contact your local agency and explain that you had "good cause." If you have an approved good cause, then you can get benefits that month without it hurting your ability to continue getting FoodShare.

topic: What a six-month report is
passage: If you are getting FoodShare, we may ask you to update your household information every six months. You can do so by completing a Six-Month Report.

topic: How to complete a six-month report
section_heading: How do I complete a Six-Month Report?
passage:
We will mail you a FoodShare Six-Month Report and Instructions, F-16076 , about a month before it is due. You can complete it:
Online: log in to ACCESS ( ACCESS in Spanish ).
By phone or in person: contact your agency .
By mail: return the form to the address listed in the box at the top of the form.

topic: What happens if a six-month report is late
section_heading: What if I turn in my Six-Month Report late?
passage: If you don’t complete all steps by the end of the month when they’re due, federal rules require that we reduce your benefits based on when we get the information. For example, if you don’t provide your documents until the 15 th of the following month, you’ll only get about half of your FoodShare.

topic: What happens if a six-month report is very late
section_heading: What if I turn in my Six-Month Report late?
passage: Your benefits will end if your form and any needed documents are more than a month late. You’ll need to reapply to start getting FoodShare again.

topic: What FSET is
page_title: Join FoodShare Employment and Training (FSET) Today!
passage: FoodShare Employment and Training (FSET) is a free program for anyone 16 and older who gets FoodShare. FSET can help you learn new job skills, get access to education and training, and find a career that interests you. Participating in FSET is also a way to meet the work requirement for FoodShare.

topic: How to enroll in FSET
page_title: Join FoodShare Employment and Training (FSET) Today!
passage: Before starting FSET, you need to enroll in FoodShare. You may know it as food stamps, QUEST card, EBT, your food card, or SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program). In Wisconsin, these are all other words for FoodShare.

topic: How to get started with FSET
page_title: Join FoodShare Employment and Training (FSET) Today!
passage: Find your FSET agency and reach out to set up an appointment for orientation to get started. A worker from your local FSET agency will meet with you to talk about your job needs and goals.

topic: Reporting change for members 60 through 64
section_heading: Rule changes for FoodShare members 60-64 years old
passage: Starting August 8, if you are 60–64, and aren’t blind or disabled, you no longer qualify for longer renewal periods.

topic: What members 60 through 64 must now do
section_heading: Rule changes for FoodShare members 60-64 years old
passage:
If you are a current member with a 36-month renewal period, you will keep your renewal date. But now you must complete both:
Six-month reports
An interview at your next renewal.

topic: Work requirement expansion
passage:
Last year federal rules expanded the work requirement for some FoodShare members.
The age range of affected members grew to 18-64, and it added parents whose children at home who are age 14 and older.

topic: FoodShare member line phone number
page_title: FoodShare: A Recipe for Good Health
passage: Call your agency or ForwardHealth Member Services at 800-362-3002 if you think someone is trying to scam you.

topic: How to manage FoodShare benefits online
page_title: FoodShare: A Recipe for Good Health
section_heading: How to manage your benefits online
passage: Only use ACCESS ( ACCESS in Spanish ) to apply for and manage your benefits. You also can use MyACCESS mobile app to get information about your benefits. If you get FoodShare benefits, you can use the ebtEDGE mobile app to access your account.

topic: What FoodShare is
page_title: FoodShare: A Recipe for Good Health
passage: You’ve probably heard of food stamps or SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program). In Wisconsin, we call the program FoodShare. The goal of this program is to stop hunger.

topic: What a FoodShare sanction is
passage: If you do not follow FoodShare basic work rules, and you do not have an exemption or a good cause reason, you will not be able to get FoodShare benefits for a period of time. This is called a sanction period.

topic: Quitting a job without good cause
section_heading: What are the basic work rules?
passage: Not quit a job of 30 or more hours per week voluntarily and without good cause (or a job with weekly earnings of $217.50 or more).

topic: How long a sanction lasts
section_heading: How long is a sanction period?
passage:
The length of a sanction period depends on how many sanctions you have:
The first sanction is for one month.
A second sanction is for three months.
A third or more sanction period is for six months.

topic: How a sanction can end early
section_heading: Can I end a sanction period early?
passage: You can end a sanction period early if you have an exemption from the FoodShare basic work rules. Call your agency right away if you have an exemption.

topic: Getting FoodShare again after a sanction ends
section_heading: Once my sanction period ends, how do I get FoodShare benefits again?
passage: You will need to reapply for FoodShare. If you are part of a household that is already getting benefits, you will need to contact your agency to have them update your case.
